title: Running Python and print()
goal: Run your first Python code and control exactly what print() shows.

cards.p: A Python program is a list of instructions. Python runs them one line at a time, from the first line down. If a line has a mistake, Python stops there and shows an error.
cards.code:
print("Line 1")
print("Line 2")

cards.p: `print()` writes text to the screen. Text goes inside quotes. Give it several values separated by commas and it prints them with a space between.
cards.code:
print("Hello")
print("Order", 1001, "ready")   # Order 1001 ready

cards.p: `sep` changes what goes between values (default: a space). `end` changes what goes at the end (default: a new line `\n`).
cards.code:
print("OA", "2026", "1001", sep="-")  # OA-2026-1001
print("Loading", end="...")
print("done")                          # Loading...done

cards.p: Anything after `#` is a comment. Python ignores it. Use comments to explain why, not what.
cards.code:
# Odoo logs use print-like output while debugging
print("debug")  # temporary

odoo: Odoo itself is a large Python program. When you start the Odoo server, everything in the terminal log is Python output.

print("A", end="")
print("B")
predict.why: sep="-" joins the first two words with a dash. end="" stops print from adding a new line, so B appears right after A.

title: Variables and types
goal: Store values in variables and know the basic types.

cards.h: A variable is a name for a value
cards.p: `=` means assign: put the value on the right into the name on the left. You can change it later.
cards.code:
qty = 5000
qty = qty + 500
print(qty)   # 5500

cards.p: Names use letters, digits and `_`, and can't start with a digit. Python style is snake_case. Names are case-sensitive: `Qty` and `qty` are different.
cards.code:
unit_price = 0.12   # good
# 2nd_order = 1    -> SyntaxError
# unit-price = 1   -> Python reads this as unit minus price

cards.p: `int` whole numbers, `float` decimals, `str` text, `bool` True/False, `None` means no value. `type()` tells you the type.
cards.code:
print(type(5000))     # <class 'int'>
print(type(0.12))     # <class 'float'>
print(type("H&M"))    # <class 'str'>
print(type(True))     # <class 'bool'>
print(type(None))     # <class 'NoneType'>

cards.p: Assign several names at once, and swap two values without a temporary variable.
cards.code:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)   # 2 1

odoo: Odoo field types map to these: fields.Integer holds an int, fields.Float a float, fields.Char a str, fields.Boolean a bool. An empty field often reads as False in Odoo, not None.

title: let, const and types
goal: Declare variables with let and const, and know JavaScript's types.

cards.p: `const` for values you won't reassign (the default choice). `let` for values that change. Avoid the old `var`.
Primitives: `number`, `string`, `boolean`, `undefined` (declared but no value), `null` (deliberately empty), plus `bigint` and `symbol`. Everything else is an object.
`const` stops you reassigning the name, but you can still change the contents of an object or array.

odoo: Odoo's JavaScript style uses const by default and let only when a value changes. You'll see this in every OWL component.

predict.why: const allows changing an array's contents, so the length is 2. typeof null is "object", a long-standing quirk.

title: Numbers and arithmetic
goal: Do arithmetic correctly, including the operators that surprise beginners.

cards.p: `+ - *` as usual. `/` always gives a float. `//` is floor division (whole part). `%` is the remainder. `**` is power.
`**` first, then `* / // %`, then `+ -`. Use brackets when in doubt; they also make code easier to read.
Computers store decimals in binary, so some results are slightly off. Use round() for display, and never compare floats with == when money matters.
`+=`, `-=`, `*=` and friends update a variable using its current value.
cards.code:
stock = 1000
stock -= 250
stock *= 2
print(stock)   # 1500

odoo: Odoo avoids float errors in money with float_round() and float_compare() using the currency's precision. Now you know why they exist.

predict.why: 7 // 2 is 3, the remainder of 7 / 2 is 1, and 2 ** 3 is 8.

title: Strings and template literals
goal: Work with strings and build text with template literals.

cards.p: Backticks allow `${…}` expressions inside the text and multi-line strings. They're the JavaScript version of Python's f-strings.
cards.code:
const qty = 1200, price = 0.35;

cards.p: Positions start at 0. `slice(start, end)` excludes end. `at(-1)` gives the last character.
Like Python, these return new strings.
cards.code:

console.log("WH/OUT/17".includes("OUT"));     // true
console.log("PO-HM-88412".split("-"));         // ["PO","HM","88412"]
console.log("7".padStart(5, "0"));            // 00007

odoo: OWL templates handle most text, but you'll use template literals for notification messages and building values in JavaScript code.

title: Strings: the basics
goal: Build, measure, index and slice strings.

cards.p: Use single or double quotes. Triple quotes allow several lines. `\n` is a new line and `\t` a tab.
cards.code:
a = 'H&M'
b = "Kohl's"   # double quotes let you use '
c = """Line 1
Line 2"""

cards.p: `+` joins strings, `*` repeats them, `len()` counts characters. You can't add a str and an int directly.
cards.code:
print("OA-" + "1001")   # OA-1001
print("-" * 10)          # ----------
print(len("ZIPPER"))     # 6
# print("Qty: " + 5000)  -> TypeError

cards.p: Each character has a position starting at 0. Negative positions count from the end: -1 is the last.
cards.code:
s = "ZIPPER"
print(s[0])    # Z
print(s[-1])   # R

cards.p: `s[start:stop]` takes characters from start up to, but not including, stop. Leave one side empty to go to the edge.
Strings are immutable. You don't edit one; you build a new one.
cards.code:
s = "zipper"
# s[0] = "Z"   -> TypeError
s = "Z" + s[1:]
print(s)   # Zipper

odoo: Odoo record names such as 'S00042' or 'WH/OUT/00017' are strings. Slicing like name[-5:] is a quick way to pull out the number part.

predict.code:

print(s[1:4], s[-1])
predict.why: Positions 1, 2 and 3 are I, P, P (the stop index 4 is not included). s[-1] is the last letter, R.

title: Conditions and equality
goal: Make decisions with if/else, and avoid JavaScript's equality traps.

cards.p: Conditions go in brackets, blocks in braces.
`==` converts types before comparing, which causes surprises. `===` compares value and type. Use `===` and `!==`.
cards.code:
console.log(0 == "");    // true  (surprise!)
console.log(0 === "");   // false

cards.p: Falsy values: `false`, `0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. Unlike Python, an empty array `[]` and empty object `{}` are truthy!
cards.code: if ([]) console.log("empty array is truthy");

cards.p: The ternary `cond ? a : b` picks a value. `??` gives a default only for null/undefined.

odoo: OWL templates use the same idea: t-if="props.record.data.state === 'done'". Strict equality avoids bugs with Odoo's false-for-empty fields.

title: String methods and f-strings
goal: Clean and format text with string methods and f-strings.

cards.p: Methods return a new string. `strip()` removes spaces at both ends.
cards.code:
s = "  kontoor  "
print(s.strip())          # kontoor
print(s.strip().upper())  # KONTOOR
print("gap inc".title())  # Gap Inc

cards.p: `replace(old, new)`, `find()` gives a position or -1, `startswith()` / `endswith()` give True or False.
cards.code:
code = "WH/OUT/00017"
print(code.replace("/", "-"))   # WH-OUT-00017
print(code.startswith("WH"))    # True
print(code.find("OUT"))         # 3

cards.p: `split(sep)` cuts a string into a list. `sep.join(list)` glues a list back into one string.
cards.code:
parts = "PO-HM-88412".split("-")
print(parts)            # ['PO', 'HM', '88412']
print(" / ".join(parts)) # PO / HM / 88412

cards.p: Put `f` before the quotes, then any expression inside `{}`. Add a format after `:` such as `.2f` (2 decimals) or `,` (thousands).
cards.code:
qty, price = 12500, 0.3456
print(f"Qty: {qty:,}")                # Qty: 12,500
print(f"Total: {qty * price:.2f}")    # Total: 4320.00

odoo: Odoo uses f-strings and _() for messages. In SQL, never build queries with f-strings; you'll learn why in the PostgreSQL lesson.

title: Arrays and array methods
goal: Use arrays and the methods you'll use daily: map, filter, reduce, find.

cards.p: `push` adds to the end, `pop` removes from the end, `includes` checks membership, `indexOf` finds a position.
`map` makes a new array by transforming each item. `filter` keeps items that pass a test. Neither changes the original.
`reduce` combines everything into one value. `find` returns the first match or undefined.
By default, sort() compares items as strings! For numbers, pass a compare function.

title: Booleans and comparisons
goal: Write true/false logic with comparisons, and, or, not.

cards.p: `== != < > <= >=`. `==` compares values; `=` assigns.
cards.code:
qty = 500
print(qty == 500)   # True
print(qty != 500)   # False
print(qty >= 1000)  # False

cards.p: `and`: both must be True. `or`: at least one True. `not` flips it. Python stops early once it knows the answer (short-circuit).
cards.code:
shipped, late = True, False
print(shipped and not late)   # True
print(late or shipped)        # True

cards.p: Python lets you write ranges naturally.
cards.code:
qty = 300
print(100 <= qty <= 500)   # True

cards.p: In conditions, these count as False: `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]`, `{}`, `None`. Everything else is True. To test for None, use `is None`.
cards.code:
note = ""
print(bool(note))      # False
value = None
print(value is None)   # True

qty = 12000

    print("Check capacity")
print("Done")   # always runs

cards.p: `else` runs when the condition is False. `elif` (else if) tests another condition. Python checks from the top and runs only the first branch that is True.
Put the most specific test first. If the first test is too wide, the later branches never run.
For a simple choice between two values, write it on one line: `a if condition else b`.
cards.code:

title: while loops
goal: Repeat work with `while` loops and make sure they stop.

cards.h: while repeats while a condition is True
cards.p: Python checks the condition before each round. When it becomes False, the loop ends and the code after it runs.
cards.code:
stock = 1000

    print("Stock now", stock)

produced = 0

    day += 1

total = 0

title: Promises
goal: Understand promises: values that arrive later, with then, catch and Promise.all.

cards.p: Talking to a server takes time. JavaScript doesn't wait and freeze; it gives you a Promise, which will later be fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error.
`then` runs when the value arrives. Whatever you return from then becomes the value for the next then.

  .then(qty => qty * 0.35)
  .then(total => console.log(total));   // 420

cards.p: If any step rejects or throws, the chain jumps to `catch`. `finally` runs either way.
cards.code:
Promise.reject(new Error("Server down"))
  .then(() => console.log("never"))
  .catch(err => console.log("Failed:", err.message))
  .finally(() => console.log("done"));

cards.p: Start several jobs at once, then wait for all of them. The result is an array in the same order. If one fails, the whole thing fails.

odoo: Every call to the server, like `this.orm.searchRead(...)`, returns a promise. In OWL code you usually await it (next lesson) instead of writing then chains.

title: List methods and slicing
goal: Grow, shrink, sort and slice lists with their methods.

cards.p: `append(x)` adds one item at the end. `extend(list)` adds many. `insert(i, x)` puts an item at a position.
cards.code:
pos = ["PO-1"]
pos.append("PO-2")
pos.extend(["PO-3", "PO-4"])
pos.insert(0, "PO-0")
print(pos)   # ['PO-0', 'PO-1', 'PO-2', 'PO-3', 'PO-4']

cards.p: `remove(x)` deletes the first matching value. `pop()` removes and returns the last item; `pop(i)` removes position i.
cards.code:
pos = ["PO-1", "PO-2", "PO-3"]
pos.remove("PO-2")
last = pos.pop()
print(pos, last)   # ['PO-1'] PO-3

cards.p: `list.sort()` changes the list itself and returns None. `sorted(list)` returns a new sorted list and leaves the original alone. Add `reverse=True` for big to small.
cards.code:
qtys = [300, 5, 1200]
print(sorted(qtys))   # [5, 300, 1200]
print(qtys)           # [300, 5, 1200]
qtys.sort(reverse=True)
print(qtys)           # [1200, 300, 5]

cards.p: Slices work like strings: `lst[start:stop]`, and `lst[::-1]` reverses. `lst[:]` or `lst.copy()` makes a copy. Plain `b = a` does not copy: both names share one list.

odoo: Recordsets have their own versions of these ideas: sorted(key=...), filtered(), and slicing like orders[:5] for the first five records.

title: async / await
goal: Write asynchronous code that reads like normal code with `async` and `await`.

cards.p: An `async` function always returns a promise. Inside it, `await` pauses that function until a promise settles, without freezing the page.
Instead of `.then(value => ...)`, write `const value = await promise;`. The code reads top to bottom. (In this app's runner you can use await directly at the top level.)
A rejected promise makes `await` throw. Catch it with try/catch, the same tool you use for normal errors.
Two awaits in a row run one after the other. If the jobs don't depend on each other, start them together and use `await Promise.all([...])`, which is faster.

odoo: OWL code loads data like this: `onWillStart(async () => { this.orders = await this.orm.searchRead("sale.order", [], ["name"]); })`. You'll write that in the OWL lessons.

predict.why: The code before the first await runs at once, so "in f" prints first. An async function returns a promise (typeof "object"), and awaiting it gives 5.

quiz.why: A rejected promise makes await throw, so try/catch handles it.

quiz.q: Two independent server calls should be…
quiz.why: Starting them together saves time.

title: Tuples and unpacking
goal: Use tuples for fixed groups of values, and unpack them into names.

cards.h: A tuple is a fixed list
cards.p: Write a tuple with round brackets. Like a list it has order and indexes, but you can't change it after creating it. Use it for values that belong together.
cards.code:
size = (5, "inch")
print(size[0])     # 5
# size[0] = 7      -> TypeError

cards.p: Put several names on the left of `=` to take the items out by position. The number of names must match.
cards.code:
po = ("PO-88412", "H&M", 12000)
number, brand, qty = po
print(brand, qty)   # H&M 12000

cards.p: A star name collects the remaining items into a list. `_` is a common name for a value you don't need.
cards.code:
first, *rest = (10, 20, 30)
print(first, rest)   # 10 [20, 30]
_, brand, _ = ("PO-1", "GAP", 500)
print(brand)         # GAP

cards.p: `return a, b` actually returns a tuple. Unpack it where you call the function. `divmod()` is a built-in example.
cards.code:
boxes, left = divmod(12345, 500)
print(boxes, left)   # 24 345
one = ("only",)       # a one-item tuple needs a comma

odoo: Odoo domains are lists of tuples, like [('state', '=', 'sale'), ('amount_total', '>', 1000)]. Selection fields are defined as tuples too: ('draft', 'Draft').

predict.why: a takes the first item, c the last, and *b collects what's in between into a list.

title: Selecting and changing the page
goal: Find elements on a web page and change their text, classes and attributes.

cards.p: The browser turns HTML into a tree of objects called the DOM (Document Object Model). JavaScript changes the page by changing these objects. From today, your code runs in a real mini page; Run shows it below your output.
cards.code:
document.body.innerHTML = "

Orders

0 orders

"; console.log(document.querySelector("h1").textContent); // Orders

cards.code:
document.querySelector("#count");      // by id
document.querySelector(".late");       // by class
document.querySelectorAll("li");       // all <li> elements

cards.p: `textContent` sets plain text (safe). `innerHTML` parses HTML; never put user input into it, or someone could inject code.
cards.code:
const p = document.querySelector("#count");
p.textContent = "3 orders";

cards.p: `classList.add/remove/toggle` changes CSS classes. `setAttribute` sets attributes. `createElement` + `append` adds new elements.

title: Dictionaries
goal: Store data by name with dictionaries: create, read, add, change and delete.

cards.p: A dictionary maps keys to values, written `{key: value}`. You look a value up by its key, not by position.
cards.code:
order = {"po": "PO-88412", "brand": "H&M", "qty": 12000}
print(order["brand"])   # H&M

cards.p: Assigning to a key adds it if it's new, or replaces the value if it exists. Keys are unique.
Reading a key that doesn't exist raises KeyError. Check first with `in`, or use `get()`, which returns None (or your default) instead.
cards.code:
order = {"brand": "GAP"}
print("qty" in order)          # False
print(order.get("qty"))        # None
print(order.get("qty", 0))     # 0

cards.p: `del d[key]` removes a key. `pop(key)` removes it and gives back the value.
cards.code:
order = {"brand": "GAP", "note": "rush", "qty": 5}
del order["note"]
qty = order.pop("qty")
print(order, qty)   # {'brand': 'GAP'} 5

odoo: Dictionaries are Odoo's daily bread: `self.env['sale.order'].create({'partner_id': 7, 'note': 'rush'})` takes a dict of field values, and `write()` does too.

predict.why: There is no "c", so get returns the default 10. 10 + 2 = 12 replaces the value of "a". get() doesn't add the key.

title: Events
goal: React to clicks, typing and form submits with event listeners.

cards.p: `element.addEventListener("click", handler)` runs the handler each time the event happens. The handler receives an event object.
The `input` event fires on each key press in a field. `ev.target` is the element, and `ev.target.value` is its text.
Submitting a form normally reloads the page. Call `ev.preventDefault()` to handle it in JavaScript instead.
Events bubble up from the clicked element to its parents. One listener on a list can handle clicks on every item: check `ev.target`.

odoo: OWL's `t-on-click="this.save"` is addEventListener written in the template. Its `.prevent` and `.stop` modifiers call preventDefault() and stopPropagation() for you.

predict.why: The click starts at the button, then bubbles up to its parent div, so button logs first, then box.

opts: Stops the browser's default action (reloading the page)

opts: save() runs immediately and its return value is passed

quiz.q: Which event fires on every key press in a text field?
quiz.why: input fires on each change; change fires when the field loses focus.

title: Dictionary methods and looping
goal: Loop over dictionaries and use their methods to count and group data.

cards.p: Looping over a dict gives its keys. `values()` gives the values. `items()` gives (key, value) pairs, which you unpack in the for line.
A classic pattern: count how many times each thing appears. `get(key, 0)` gives 0 the first time.
`setdefault(key, [])` returns the list for that key, creating it if needed. Then you append to it.
`update(other)` copies keys from another dict, replacing existing ones. Dicts keep the order in which keys were added.

odoo: This counting and grouping is what read_group does in the database. In Python, you'll often build dicts like {partner_id: total} before writing a report or a summary.

predict.why: a starts at 1 and is counted twice (3). b starts from the default 0 (1).

quiz.why: Looping over a dict gives its keys. Use items() for pairs.

title: Practice: a to-do list in plain JavaScript
goal: Build a small to-do list in plain JavaScript, and feel why frameworks like OWL exist.

cards.p: Keep the data in a JavaScript array (the state). The page is just a picture of that state.
Write one function that rebuilds the list from the state. After every change to the state, call it again.
Event handlers only change the state and call render(). Use `data-` attributes so a click knows which item it belongs to.

// on click: find the todo by id, flip done, render()

cards.p: You must remember to call render() every time, and rebuilding everything is slow for big lists. OWL solves both: it re-renders automatically when reactive state changes, and only updates what changed.

odoo: This 'state → render' idea is exactly how OWL components work in Odoo. Tomorrow you'll write the same kind of thing as an OWL component, without a manual render().

predict.why: Changing the array doesn't change the page. Only after render() runs again does the page show 3 items.

title: Sets
goal: Use sets to remove duplicates and compare groups of values.

cards.p: Write a set with braces, or convert a list with `set()`. Duplicates disappear. A set has no order and no indexes.
cards.code:
brands = set(["GAP", "H&M", "GAP"])
print(len(brands))   # 2
empty = set()        # {} would be an empty dict!

cards.p: `in` is very fast on a set, even with millions of items. `add()` and `discard()` change it.
cards.code:

shipped.add("PO-3")
shipped.discard("PO-9")   # no error if missing
print("PO-2" in shipped)  # True

cards.p: `|` union (in either), `&` intersection (in both), `-` difference (in the first, not the second).
Set items (and dict keys) must be unchangeable types: numbers, strings, tuples. A list can't go in a set. To print a set in a fixed order, use `sorted()`.

odoo: Odoo recordsets support the same operators: `orders_a | orders_b` (union) and `orders_a & orders_b` (intersection), and they also remove duplicates.

predict.why: Union has each value once. a - b keeps 1 and 2. Only 3 is in both, so the intersection has 1 item.

quiz.why: Empty braces make a dict. Use set() for an empty set.

quiz.q: What does {"a", "b"} & {"b", "c"} give?

title: What OWL is: your first component
goal: Create and mount your first OWL 3 component with a template and a signal.

cards.p: OWL is Odoo's UI framework. You write components: classes that describe a piece of the screen with a template. OWL turns the template into DOM and keeps it up to date. In this runner, OWL 3 is loaded as the global `owl`.
Extend `Component` and give it a `static template`. The `xml` helper lets you write the template inline, which is handy for learning.

cards.h: mount() puts it on the page
cards.p: `mount(Component, target)` creates the component and adds it to the target element. It returns a promise, so await it before you look at the page.
cards.code:

console.log(document.querySelector("h2").textContent);   // Hello, Asif!

cards.p: A `signal(value)` is reactive state. Read it by calling it: `this.count()`. Change it with `.set()`. When it changes, OWL re-renders only what depends on it. In templates, always write `this.` before component fields and methods.

odoo: Odoo 20's web client is a tree of OWL 3 components. In Odoo, templates usually live in XML files (static template = "my_module.MyComponent"), and you rarely call mount() yourself: the web client mounts your component through a registry.
owl2: OWL 2 used `this.state = useState({ count: 0 })` and templates read `state.count` without `this.`. OWL 3 replaces useState with signals (or `proxy`), and template expressions read the component through `this.`.

predict.why: mount() returns the component. Setting the signal makes OWL re-render the span, so the second read shows 800.

title: Comprehensions
goal: Build lists, dicts and sets in one readable line with comprehensions.

cards.p: `[expression for item in items]` builds a new list. It replaces the pattern 'empty list, loop, append'.
cards.code:
qtys = [1200, 500, 3400]
doubled = [q * 2 for q in qtys]
print(doubled)   # [2400, 1000, 6800]

cards.p: Add `if condition` at the end to keep only some items.
cards.code:
qtys = [1200, 500, 3400, 800]
big = [q for q in qtys if q >= 1000]
print(big)   # [1200, 3400]

cards.p: Use braces with `key: value` for a dict, or braces with one expression for a set.
cards.code:
brands = ["gap", "h&m", "gap"]
upper = {b.upper() for b in brands}       # set
lengths = {b: len(b) for b in brands}     # dict
print(sorted(upper), lengths)

cards.p: A choice inside the expression uses `a if cond else b`. If a comprehension needs more than one line of thinking, a normal loop is clearer.
cards.code:

title: Props
goal: Pass data from a parent component to a child with props, and declare them with `useProps`.

cards.p: A parent uses a child by writing a capitalised tag in its template, and lists the class in `static components`.
Each attribute on a component tag is a prop, and its value is JavaScript evaluated in the parent. Text needs inner quotes: `po="'PO-1'"`. Parent fields need `this.`: `qty="this.qty()"`.
In OWL 3, a component only sees the props it asks for with `useProps`. Give it a schema with types from `t`; `.optional(default)` makes a prop optional with a default value.
A child must never change its props. Reads are reactive: when the parent re-renders with a new value, the child updates. Type checks only run in dev mode: `mount(App, el, { dev: true })`.

odoo: Every Odoo field widget receives standard props such as `record`, `name` and `readonly`. In Odoo 20's CharField you can see `props = useProps(charFieldProps)`, with types like `t.string().optional()`.
owl2: In OWL 2 every component had `this.props` automatically, and you described them with `static props = { ... }` and `static defaultProps`. OWL 3 ignores those: use `props = useProps({ ... })` with `t` types and `.optional(default)`.
